div.head: Frag. II
div.p: Column 43 to make use of the accusation, so allow me too to make my defence in the way I have chosen and as I am able. And let none of you interrupt me while I am speaking with Why are you telling us this? nor add anything of your own to the accusation, but rather to the defence Desunt col. 43 versus fere quindecim et col. 44 versus fere decem.

div.head: Frag. III
div.p: Column 44 Nor does the law give anyone who wishes the power to join in accusingσυγκατηγορεῖν Sauppe. those on trialκρινομένων Boeckh, Sauppe. while forbidding him to join in their defence. But so as not to spend, ἀναλώσω Babington. before the matter itself, a great many words, I shall proceed to the defenceἀπολογίαν Boeckh, Sauppe. itself, after praying to the gods to help me and save me from the present trial, and asking of you, gentlemen of the jury, this: first Deest col. 45 fere tota.

Source is Pap. Ardenianus.Column 2 And he had slaves of Ariston in the works; and he himself testified to this for you in the court, when this man had his suit against Archestratides.Ἀρχεστρατίδην Babington.

For such is the business of Ariston here: he οὗτος Shilleto: αὐτὸς Schneidewin. goes about summoning everybody, and those who do not give him money he brings to trial and accuses, while all who are willing to pay,ὁπόσοι et ἀποτίνειν Babington. he lets go; and the money he gives to Theomnestus;Ἀρίστωνος usque ad Θεομνήστῳ plerumque restituit Schneidewin. and that man takes it and buys slaves, and supplies him with provisions, as one does for pirates, and gives him for each Column 3 slave an obol a day, so that he may be an immortal informer.

It is right, gentlemen of the jury, to examine the matter starting from there too, from the charges which they themselves made at the very first in the Assembly. For theοἱ add. Schneidewin. relatives sentἀπέστειλαν ἐπέστειλαν Blass. me in writing both the impeachment and the charges which they brought against me in the Assembly when they were bringing in the impeachment, in which it was written that Lycurgus says, claiming to have heard it from the members of the household,οἰκείων ἀκηκοέναι Babington. that I, following along when Charippus was marrying the woman, urged her not to go near πλησιάσει Schneidewin: πλησιάσῃ A. Charippus but to keep herself safe.

But the very thing that, both to my Column 4 friends and to the relatives οἰκείους Babington. of my own immediately εὐθὺς Blass: τότε Babington. on arriving, I said, I also now say to you,λέγω Schneidewin: ἐρῶ Babington. namely that, if these things are true, I admit that I have done all the other things as well that are writtenγεγραμμένα Babington. in the impeachment. But that they are false ψευδῆ Schneidewin. is, I think, οἶμαι Caesar. easy for everyone to see. ἰδεῖν Caesar: γνῶναι Patakis. For who of those in the city is so unreasoning,

as to believe theseἐστι et sq. Babington, sedτούτοις τοῖς Blass:τοιούτοις Babington. words? For it was necessary,ἀνάγκη γὰρ ἦν Sauppe:ἦν om. Blass. gentlemen of the jury, first that a muleteer and a guide should follow the carriage which was taking the woman, Column 5 and then that the boys escorting her should follow, and Dioxippus too; for he too was in attendance, because she was a widow being given in marriage.

Then did I come to such a pitch of madness that, when so many other people were following along, and Dioxippus and Euphraeus his training partnerπροσγυμναστοῦ προγυμναστοῦ Westermann. too, who are admittedly the strongest of the Greeks, I neither felt ashamed to speak such words about a free woman in everyone's hearing, norοὔτ’ . . . οὔτʼ Sauppe:οὐκ . . . οὐδʼ Blass. feared that I would be killed on the spot by strangling?πνιγόμενος Kenyon: ἀπαγόμενος Babington, Colin. For who would have put up with such things about his own Column 6 sister, hearing what these men allege me to have said, andκαὶ Schneidewin: ἆρʼ Babington. not have killedἀπέκτεινε ἀπεκώλυσε Colin. the speaker?

But the crowning pointἀπούων usque ad κεφάλαιον plerumque restituit Babington. of all, ἁπάντων Sauppe. asὡς Blass:ὧν Colin. I said a little earlier πρότερον Sauppe. too, is that Charippus, it seems, came to such a degree of stupidity that, though first, as they say, the woman told him beforehand that she had sworn an oath with me, and then again he heard me urging herτοῦτο usque adαὐτῇ Babington. to abideἐμμείνειεν Herwerden: ἐμμενεῖ ἐν Schneidewin. by the oaths which she had sworn, he still took theτὴν Babington: ὅμως Blass. woman? And would these things seem to you to have been done either by that madman Orestes Ὀρέστης Blass. or by Margites, the most foolish of all?

But I think, gentlemen of the jury, that in trials the accusers have many Column 7 advantages over the defendants. For the former, because the trial carries no risk for them, easily say whatever they like and tell lies, while those on trial, because of their fear, forget to mention many even of the things they have actually done.

Then, when they get to speak first,πρότερον τὸν πρότερον Colin: πρότεροι Patakis. they not only state the just arguments that they themselves have about the matter, but they also concoct false slanders against those on trial and drive them away from their defence; so that one of two things happens to them: either, while Column 8 defending themselvesἀπολογουμένοις usque adδιαστρέφουσιν plerumque restituit Babington. against the extraneous slanders, they find their defence on the matter itself left behind,ἀπολελεῖφθαι Schneidewin. or, by not rememberingἢ et μεμνημένοις Shilleto. theτῶν περὶ τῶν Babington. accusations made earlier, they leave the impressionοἴησιν Schneidewin:οὕτω δόξαν Blass. with the jurors that what was said is true.

And besides this, they slander in advance those who are going to help the defendants,τοῖς φεύγουσι Caesar. and the defence of the accused himself they distort;See note onἀπολογουμένοις above. just as Ariston Ἀρίστων Sauppe. here attempted ἐνεχείρησε Schneidewin. to do ποιῆσαι Blass: που Kenyon. in the prosecution,κατηγορία Babington. he who does not evenὃς οὐδʼ Blass:οὐδʼ Kayser. allow me to benefit ἀπολαύειν Sudhaus: ἀπολογίαν Blass. from those coming forward on my behalf andδίδωσι usque adκαὶ Blass. intending to join in my defence.συναπολογησομένων Kayser. And why should these men not speak in my defence?διὰ usque ad ἀπολογῶνται Blass: ἀπολογήσονται Fuhr. Is it Column 9 not justδίκαιόν ἐστι Sauppe. for their relatives and friends to help those on trial? Or is there anything in the city more democratic than this, that those who are able to speak should help those citizens who are unable when they are in danger?

But you have not only made your speeches about my advocates, you also lay down the order of my defence; and you instruct the jurors on what they ought to listen to and καὶ add. Kayser:ἀκούειν del. Schneidewin. bid me plead in my defence, and on what they ought not to allow me to speak. And how is this fair, that you should make the prosecution as you wished, Column 10 but, knowing in advance the just arguments I have to make against your lies, should take my defence away from me?

And you accuse me in the impeachment of overthrowing the democracy by breaking the laws, while you yourself, leaping over all ἅπαντας Blass. the laws,νόμους usque adτραγῳδίας plerumque restituit Babington. have lodged an impeachment about matters for which public indictments lie before the Thesmothetae under the laws, so that, first, you might enter without risk into the trial, and then that you might be freeἐξῇ σοι Kayser. to put tragic scenesSee note on νόμους above. in writing into theγράψαι εἰς τὴν Blass. impeachment, such as οἵασπερ Kayser. you have now written, you whoὅς μʼ Blass. accuse me on the ground that manyπολλὰς μὲν Sauppe. women I causeποιῶ Blass., unmarried, at home, to grow old,ἀγάμους ἔνδον καταγηράσκειν Babington. and many to live with men πολλὰς usque ad οἷς Sauppe. Column 11 to whom it is not fitting, contrary to the laws.

So then οὐκοῦν Babington: οὔκουν Schneidewin. you cannot name any other woman in the city to whom I am the cause of these things; but as for the woman about whom you have now made your accusation, did you thinkPostᾤου add. οὐ Kirchhoff. it fitting that she should live, given in marriage, with Charippus, one of the citizens, or that she should grow old at home unmarried, she who was given in marriage at once, Euphemus adding a talent of silver for her, clearly not out of wickedness but out of kindness?

This man, then, is free, Oὦ add. Babington, quod dubium an A supra versum habeat. men of the jury, both to say whatever he wishes and to tell lies against me; but you, I think, ought to judge me not from the prosecutor's Column 12 slanders, but after examining the whole life that I have lived. For it is not possible for anyone in the city, whether he is wicked or decent, to escape the notice of your community; rather, the time that has passed is for each man the most exact witness of his character, especially in the case of charges such as this one is.

For those of the offences which, in every stage of τῇ Sauppe. a man's life, it is possibleἐνδέχεται usque adτοιοῦτος plerumque restituit Babington. to commit, these one must examine on the basis of the very chargeἐγκλήματος Blass: ἀξιώματος Babington. which one faces; adultery, however, cannot be begun by a man ἄνθρωπον olim Jensen: ἀρξάμενον Babington. from fifty years of age onwards, but either he has long been of that sort,See note onἐενδέχεται above. which let these men prove, Column 13 or the charge is likely to be false.

Now I, gentlemen of the jury, having spent all my time with you in the city, have never incurred any disgraceful charge, nor have I ever had a complaint against any of the citizens, nor have I been a defendant in any lawsuit, nor have I prosecuted another; but I have spent all my time keeping horses with ambition, beyond my means and beyond my own property. And I have been crowned by all the knights for bravery, and by my fellow officers.

For you, gentlemen of the jury, Column 14 first elected me phylarch, and then hipparch for Lemnos; and I held command there for two years, alone of all who have ever been hipparch, and I stayed on there for a third year in addition, not wishing to exact headlong from citizens who were in financial difficulty the pay for the horsemen.

And during this time none of the people there brought any charge against me, either private or public, but I was crowned with three crowns by the people in Hephaestia and with others by the people in Myrina; and these things ought χρὴ Blass. to be εἶναι Sauppe. proofs to you, for this Column 15 trial, that theαἱ add. Babington. charges against me are false. For it is not possible that a man who is wicked in Athens should be good in Lemnos, nor did you send me there as being such a man, when you entrusted two of your own cities to me.

What I had to say on my own behalf, then, gentlemen of the jury, you have more or less heard. But since the prosecutor, who is not inexperienced in speaking and is used to contending often in court, called advocates to help him ruin one of the citizens unjustly, I too beg and entreat you to bid me also to call those who will speak Column 16 for me in so great a trial, and to listen with goodwill, if any of my relatives or friends is able to help me,

since I am your fellow citizen, a private man and not used to speaking, and am on trial and in danger not only of death, for that is the least thing to those who reason rightly, but of being banished and, when dead, not even being buried in my native land. So if you bid me, gentlemen of the jury, I call someone to help me. Come up, Theophilus, and speak with me whatever you can; the jurors bid you.
